headline: High-risk filesystem and network overlap: AutoGen can write and execute code while social-auto-upload can push account-linked media, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write the filesystem and ingest file/stdin content, while social-auto-upload consumes local media/account files and uses CLI/API flows. A shared workspace or copied outputs create a plausible instruction-hijack path, though no MCP or clipboard bridge is documented. The interaction is possible in default orchestration, but not proven to be raw-content parsing.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same working directory, prompt-like content in files can influence downstream actions.
IF AutoGen outputs text that social-auto-upload later parses as commands or metadata, injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Use separate working directories for each agent.
Strip instructions from any file passed between agents.
Require a human review step before upload commands.
Disable automatic file-to-command parsing in the uploader.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all inter-agent artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen handles application data and model-provider API keys, and social-auto-upload touches account data plus media files. If they share a workspace, AutoGen can read sensitive files and social-auto-upload can transmit them via network egress to external services. The profiles do not show isolation by default, so leakage is plausible in ordinary use.
conditions: IF the two agents share a directory containing account data or secrets, AutoGen can read them.
IF social-auto-upload is run on files produced by AutoGen, those contents may be uploaded to third-party platforms.
mitigations: Keep secrets in a separate directory from shared artifacts.
Rotate any exposed API keys before pairing the agents.
Use a throwaway account for upload testing.
Review the exact files queued for upload before execution.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem sandboxing.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen has unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, while social-auto-upload has no filesystem write or shell capability. There is little direct write-write conflict, but both can still contend over shared files or account state if the operator places them in the same workspace. The blast radius is limited because only one agent can mutate local files.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to use the same output directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF the uploader reads files while AutoGen is still writing them, partial-state errors can occur.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Serialize runs so only one agent writes at a time.
Use atomic rename for generated media files.
Check file timestamps before upload.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared artifacts.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate code, plans, or facts that social-auto-upload may treat as authoritative input for uploads or account actions. Because the uploader has network egress and account-data access, a mistaken or malicious AutoGen output can cascade into irreversible public posting or account misuse. No verification mechanism is documented between the pair, so the safer choice is the higher severity.
conditions: IF social-auto-upload consumes AutoGen-generated captions, paths, or credentials without validation, errors can propagate to live uploads.
IF AutoGen produces a malformed or malicious upload plan, the uploader may execute it.
mitigations: Require human approval for every upload batch.
Validate captions, paths, and account targets against a schema.
Compare generated plans against a whitelist of allowed actions.
Run a dry-run mode before live posting.
requires-engineering: add signed handoff artifacts between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen is a general-purpose framework that can process application data and secrets, while social-auto-upload handles account data and media for external platforms. If regulated or personal data is placed into the shared workflow, the uploader's broad network egress can move it to third-party services without any documented residency or retention controls. The profiles do not show a compliance boundary, so the mismatch is material.
conditions: IF personal or regulated data is included in the media or account metadata, it may be transmitted to external platforms.
IF the operator relies on differing retention or deletion expectations, compliance gaps can arise.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from upload inputs.
Document retention and deletion expectations for both tools.
Use test accounts and synthetic media only.
Review platform privacy settings before posting.
requires-engineering: implement policy checks for data residency and retention.
